segments.text: When you open chat GBT and type a message, you communicate in words,
but the AI on the other end doesn't actually see it that way.
Underneath the interface, the system splits your text into smaller puzzle pieces, called tokens.
Each of these tokens carries an embedding.
That's a specific row of numbers representing the starting static dictionary definition of that exact piece of text.
The challenge is that human language isn't static.
It's subjective and constantly shifting based on the situation.
The AI has to find a way to make those fixed rows of numbers flexible enough to understand exactly what you mean.
Look at this diagram showing the two main problems context must solve.
Problem one.
The exact same word can mean completely different things.
Take light.
In please turn on the light, it means brightness.
In the empty suitcase felt light, it means not heavy.
The AI has to look at the surrounding clues, like turn on or empty suitcase, to figure out which definition you intend.
Problem two is pronouns.
A single pronoun can point to entirely different things depending on the sentence.
The cat was thirsty, so it drank the milk.
Here, it is the cat.
But right, the milk was fresh, so the cat drank it, and suddenly it is the milk.
The AI has to map the connections between thirsty and drank versus fresh and drank, to resolve what the pronoun is actually targeting.
In both cases, the surrounding words help AI figure out the meaning.
Contextual clues are the only tools it has to deduce your true intent.
Using contextual clues means the system actually has to keep track of them over the length of your message.
Earlier AI architectures struggled to do this.
Look at how earlier AI read text, moving strictly from left to right, one word at a time.
The issue with reading linearly is by the time it reaches a pronoun like it at the end of a passage, the system loses its connection to earlier context words.
This inability to retain long-range context created a hard ceiling for how well a machine could comprehend language.
To move forward, the entire reading process had to be redesigned.
That redesign arrived in 2017.
When researchers at Google published a paper titled, attention is all you need.
It introduced the transformer, which is the architecture that puts the T in chat GPT.
Here we see how a transformer reads.
Instead of moving sequentially, it processes all the tokens in your message simultaneously.
Because every word is visible at the same time, a word at the end can instantly draw context from a word at the beginning, even across several words.
This breaks down how the transformer pulls that off.
First is attention, weighing information from relevant words and blending that context back into the target token's numbers.
Second is transformation, using learned patterns to further process those blended numbers, physically changing the mathematical value of the token.
The transformer resolves ambiguity by actively updating each token's underlying math, using the clues surrounding it.
Let's apply those mechanics back to the light and it problems we started with.
Here, attention and transformation use clues like turn on and empty to mathematically separate the definitions of light.
For pronouns, it runs the same process, weighing surrounding verbs to point it back to the thirsty cat or the milk.
Because the AI constantly updates a word's literal meaning using the words around it, it can process language that isn't literal at all.
That same mathematical blending of context gives the system the clues it needs to decipher abstract concepts like sarcasm and idioms.
But, identifying contextual clues only provides the correct meaning.
To fully comprehend a sentence, the AI must still solve for structure.
The words alone aren't enough, their specific sequence carries distinct meaning.
Consider this example, dog bites man versus man bites dog.
Both have the exact same tokens but describe entirely different events.
Without position data, the text is processed as a scrambled pile.
Positional encoding solves this by mathematically stamping a specific number onto each token to track its sequence.
When you combine positional data with the ability to instantly connect surrounding context, it turns out that attention is all you need.
Artificial intelligence relies entirely on calculating these complex, invisible relationships between our words to accurately interpret our messages.
